summary: Complements other multicast security threat analyses by describing threats to Protocol Independent Multicast (PIM) that come from hosts attached to router interfaces. It looks at what a misbehaving or malicious host on a router's local network could do to the multicast routing infrastructure. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Think of a school hallway where a student pretends to be a teacher to confuse the class schedule. This lists the tricks a user's computer might play on the routers that deliver group broadcasts.

subtitle: Protecting multicast routers from misbehaving hosts on the same network.

tldr.problem: Hosts on the same local network as a multicast router can send forged PIM messages to disrupt multicast service or interfere with the router's operation.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC catalogs specific attacks (forged Register messages, fake neighbor claims, elected as DR) and methods to defend against them: passive mode, IPsec, or IP filtering.
tldr.outcome: Administrators can harden multicast networks by understanding threats and choosing appropriate defenses based on their topology.

today: RFC 5294 is an Informational RFC and remains an important security reference for operators deploying multicast on LANs. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Introduction to Host-Interface Threats
sections.content:
Protocol Independent Multicast (PIM) is used by routers to coordinate the delivery of group messages to all subscribers (multicast). When PIM runs on a router's interface connecting to hosts, those hosts can send crafted PIM messages to interfere with the routing.

The RFC defines host threats as attacks where nodes (malicious hosts or illegitimate routers) use PIM to attack or deny service to other hosts or legitimate routers on the same link, or to bypass router controls by sending fake PIM Register messages.

Unlike attacks on the overall multicast infrastructure, these are local-link threats: a compromised host on your LAN can disrupt multicast delivery to your entire network.
sections.eli5: PIM is how routers decide who gets to watch a broadcast. A bad host on your network can send fake PIM messages to trick routers and stop everyone from watching.

sections.title: How Hosts Can Attack PIM
sections.content:
The RFC describes six main attack vectors: (1) Malicious hosts can send PIM Register messages directly to Rendezvous Points, bypassing router rate-limits or reaching foreign RPs. (2) Any host can become a PIM neighbor by sending Hello messages, gaining the ability to send other PIM messages. (3) Some PIM implementations don't verify that PIM messages come from known neighbors, allowing spoofed attacks. (4) An attacker that becomes a neighbor can win Designated Router (DR) election, controlling which data gets forwarded and registered. (5) Similarly, in BIDIR-PIM, an attacker can become the Designated Forwarder using spoofed Offer messages. (6) PIM Assert messages can be spoofed to force a host to forward (or block) traffic for a specific group.

In BIDIR-PIM specifically, the absence of Reverse Path Forwarding (RPF) checks allows attackers to use spoofed source addresses in multicast packets, evading detection.
sections.eli5: A bad computer can trick routers by: sending fake join requests, claiming to be a router, winning fake elections, stealing the right to forward traffic, or sending messages with fake sender addresses.

sections.title: Real-World Attack Scenarios
sections.content:
Denial-of-service on the link: An attacker becomes DR by sending Hello and Offer messages, then refuses to forward multicast data onto the link, or discards PIM Join/Prune messages so no one receives anything. Alternatively, it sends spoofed Assert messages claiming to be a legitimate router, preventing others from forwarding.

Denial-of-service beyond the link: An attacker sends its own Register messages directly to the Rendezvous Point, either bypassing rate-limits (causing DoS upstream) or spoofing source addresses if ingress filtering isn't deployed. In BIDIR-PIM, spoofed source addresses make the attack harder to trace.

Integrity and confidentiality attacks: A DR can modify data packets before Register-encapsulating them upstream. An attacker forming a neighbor adjacency or spoofing a neighbor's IP address can send Assert messages to intercept external traffic, modify it, and forward a corrupted version to the LAN.
sections.eli5: An attacker can: stop everyone on the network from receiving broadcasts, flood the upstream network with fake messages, or modify the data before others see it.

sections.title: Defenses and Mitigation
sections.content:
The RFC proposes three main defenses, effective in different scenarios. Passive mode: For networks with only one PIM router, disable PIM on the host interface entirely. Hosts can still send and receive multicast, but no PIM Hello or other PIM messaging happens, eliminating all host-interface PIM attacks.

IPsec: Encrypt and authenticate all PIM messages between routers using IPsec, preventing hosts from forging them. This is suitable when multiple routers exist on the link. However, manual key setup is tedious and automatic negotiation (GDOI) adds complexity.

IP filtering: Block IP protocol 103 (all PIM messages) at the edge, either on the router's access list or directly on Ethernet switch ports. This is effective even with multiple routers if the switches filter host ports. The trade-off is that Ethernet switches need more sophisticated layer-3 filtering.

The RFC provides a summary table (Section 4.4) showing which defenses address each vulnerability and their suitability for single-router versus multi-router links.
sections.eli5: Three ways to stop these attacks: (1) turn off PIM messaging on that network if you only have one router, (2) encrypt all PIM messages between routers, or (3) have the network equipment block all PIM messages from reaching hosts.
